title: Latching pucks: where does the energy go?

stimulus.title: Latching pucks
stimulus.html: Puck A, of mass m, slides at speed v₀ toward puck B, of mass M, which is at rest on level, frictionless ice. The pucks latch together when they collide. A student repeats the experiment with pucks B of different masses M, keeping m and v₀ the same.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: As M is made larger, does the fraction of A's initial kinetic energy that remains as kinetic energy after the collision increase, decrease or stay the same? Justify your answer without manipulating equations.

rubric.point: States that the momentum of the system is the same for every M (no net external force), so a larger total mass must move more slowly after latching.
accept: same momentum shared by more mass

rubric.point: Reasons that kinetic energy depends on the speed squared, so the slower, heavier pair carries less kinetic energy for the same momentum.
accept: K = ½(m + M)v², and v falls faster than the mass grows
for a fixed momentum, more mass means less kinetic energy

parts.sample: It decreases. With no net external force on the two pucks, their total momentum after latching equals A's initial momentum whatever M is. A larger total mass carrying the same momentum must move more slowly, and since kinetic energy goes as the speed squared but only linearly with mass, the heavier, slower pair has less kinetic energy. More of A's kinetic energy becomes thermal energy and sound in the latch.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Starting with conservation of momentum, derive an expression for the fraction K_f/K_i of A's initial kinetic energy that remains after the collision, in terms of m and M.

rubric.point: Starts from conservation of momentum: mv₀ = (m + M)v_f, so v_f = mv₀/(m + M).
accept: p before = p after for the two pucks

rubric.point: Writes K_i = ½mv₀² and K_f = ½(m + M)v_f² with the derived v_f substituted.

parts.sample: The net external force on A and B is zero, so mv₀ = (m + M)v_f and v_f = mv₀/(m + M). Then K_f = ½(m + M)v_f² = ½m²v₀²/(m + M), and K_i = ½mv₀², so K_f/K_i = m/(m + M).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how your expression in part (b) supports your claim in part (a). Then use it to determine the fraction of the kinetic energy lost when M = m.

rubric.point: Explains that M appears only in the denominator, so increasing M decreases m/(m + M), consistent with (a).
For M = m, the fraction remaining is ½, so half of the kinetic energy is lost.

parts.sample: M appears only in the denominator of m/(m + M), so a larger M gives a smaller fraction of kinetic energy remaining, as claimed. For M = m the fraction remaining is m/(2m) = ½, so half of A's kinetic energy is lost in the collision.
